title: HOSA Forensic Science: Forensic Anthropology - Forensic Anthropology - Biological Profiling - Stature
subject: Forensic Anthropology

questions.q: Stature (living height) can be mathematically estimated by measuring the length of specific bones and applying regression formulas. Which category of bones is best suited for these calculations?
questions.explain: Long bones (e.g., femur, tibia, humerus, radius) comprise the primary vertical length of the limbs and mathematically correlate most strongly with the overall height of a person.
questions.subject: Forensic Anthropology

questions.q: A forensic investigator calculates the stature of a victim using the equation $$Height = 2.47 \times (femur\;length) + 54.10$$. Why must the anthropologist first know the individual's sex and ancestry before relying heavily on this specific mathematical formula?
options: Because flat bones shrink at different rates during decomposition depending on sex and ancestry.
Because the ratios of limb proportions to total body height differ across varying sexes and ancestral backgrounds.
Because long bones of males only grow until age 15, while those of females grow until age 21.
Because epiphyseal fusion prevents accurate long bone measurement in individuals over 30.
questions.explain: Mathematical regression formulas are specific to the population from which they are derived. Differences in body proportions (e.g., limb length to torso ratios) exist among different sexes and populations of varying ancestral origins.
questions.subject: Forensic Anthropology

questions.q: What specialized piece of equipment is standardly utilized in the forensic laboratory to accurately measure the maximum length of long bones for stature calculations?
questions.explain: An osteometric board is designed specifically for taking the maximum lengths of large long bones like the femur or tibia securely and accurately.
